newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Howard says no plan to sell all of Telstra.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Howard says no plan to sell all of Telstra.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday his government had not changed its policy on the partial sale of state-owned telecoms firm Telstra.
"The government has not taken any decision to sell off the whole of Telstra," Howard said.

"Any suggestion by anybody that the Cabinet has taken a decision to sell more is completely wrong and ill-informed," Howard told reporters. "The only policy commitment we have is a commitment to sell one third...and nothing has changed."

The Liberal-National government wants to sell one third of Telstra in its first term of office, with foreign ownership of that tranche limited to one third. The sell-off would raise an estimated A$8.0 billion.
But the Labor opposition and minor parties which control the balance of power in Parliament's upper house, the Senate, have pledged to block the sell-off.

Communications Minister Senator Richard Alston said in a weekend television interview that the government hoped to eventually sell all of Telstra. His comment was the first time that the conservative government, elected in March this year, had expressed any desire to completely offload the carrier.
Howard said he was not convinced there was a public benefit in selling more than one third of Telstra.
"I would like to see how the third sale goes before I turn my mind to the sale of any more," he said.

Howard said the best scenario may be for a "period" where one third of Telstra is owned by Australians and two thirds by the government and then "down the track" consider the possibility of selling more of the telecommunications carrier.
"That has always been our position," he said.
Howard said any decision to sell more of Telstra would be the subject of a policy that his government would take to an election, which is not due until mid 1999.

"The only decision that the government has taken is the policy that we took to the last election. Cabinet has not even discussed, even in the remotest theoretical way, the possibility of selling off any other portion of Telstra," Howard said.
"If there were any intention to go any further that would be the subject of an explicit policy at a subsequent election."
